newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia snubs Montenegro funeral as division grows.
newsitem.headline: Serbia snubs Montenegro funeral as division grows.

text.p: The Yugoslav foreign minister failed to attend the funeral of his Montenegrin counterpart on Saturday, worsening tension between Belgrade and its federation partner, local officials said.
Janko Jeknic, 47, a respected career diplomat who helped tiny Montenegro pursue a pro-Western economic and political policy, died in a car crash on Friday morning.

Hundreds attended the funeral in the capital of Montenegro, the small southern republic which along with its dominant neighbour Serbia makes up what is left of Yugoslavia after other republics followed a bloody path to independence.
But Yugoslav Federation Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic did not attend and instead sent a junior deputy.

Analysts said the snub reflected Belgrade's displeasure at Montenegran calls for the Serbian government to compromise over disputed local elections in November that have led to more than two months of street protests across Serbia.
The opposition in Serbia says it was defrauded of victory in 14 cities and towns by Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's socialists, a claim backed by international inspectors.
Socialist hard-liners have prevented the opposition taking its seats and neutered attempts to reform Serbia's shattered economy in a bit to keep hold of the state's dwindling purse.
In contrast tiny Montenegro has pushed through a reform programme and believes it must lesson Serbia's influence if it is to gain access to vital Western investment.

"If anyone, including Milosevic, thinks we can be diverted from our Western political and economic orientation, he is making a very sorry mistake," a senior political source told Reuters on Saturday. "If Serbia cannot or does not want to keep up, then it is its own problem."
Montenegro, home to only half a million people and Serbia's only outlet to the sea, has privatised some 90 percent of its economy, albeit mostly via sales to members of the ruling elite.
"Everything here is now for sale. If you have money, you can buy industry, banks, anything, you name it," the source said.
In Podgorica government officials, citizens and private entrepreneurs have some optimism, unlike in Serbia where the economy is a landscape of unrelieved gloom.
"You have to understand that after 50 years of communism, which I did not trust, the future of my family is in my own hands," said Petar Tomasevic, a boutique owner in Podgorica.
But the optimism is overshadowed by fears the West might re-impose sanctions on Belgrade for refusing to accept the election results, damaging Montenegro along with it.

"The tens of millions of dollars we were expecting from the West in the form of various contracts in the past few months have failed to materialise. To some it is a paltry sum, to us it's a lot of money," the political source said.

"We have no option, we have no future other than integration with the West," said Jeknic before his death. "The East might be our trading partner, but certainly not a source of ideology. It is the West where we gain our strength from."
There are even whispers ties to Belgrade could be loosened.
"We do not have to talk about secession per se, but we can and will certainly consider making our relationship with Belgrade into a loose confederation," the political source said.
